Given the limitations of this research (being a pilot study of a topic not addressed in ICU with few patients) should be carried further study with sufficient power to test this hypothesis.

title: Effect of adjuvant trastuzumab treatment in conventional clinical setting: an observational retrospective multicenter Italian study
abstract: Clinical trials have shown the efficacy of trastuzumab-based adjuvant therapy in HER2-positive breast cancers, but routine clinical use awaits evaluation of compliance, safety, and effectiveness. Adjuvant trastuzumab-based therapy in routine clinical use was evaluated in the retrospective study GHEA, recording 1,002 patients treated according to the HERA protocol between March 2005 and December 2009 in 42 Italian oncology departments; 874 (87.23 %) patients completed 1-year trastuzumab treatment. In 128 patients (12.77 %), trastuzumab was withdrawn due to cardiac or non-cardiac toxicity (28 and 29 patients, respectively), disease progression (5 patients) or the clinician's decision (66 patients). In addition, 156 patients experienced minor non-cardiac toxicities; 10 and 44 patients showed CHF and decreased LVEF, respectively, at the end of treatment. Compliance and safety of adjuvant trastuzumab-based therapy in Italian hospitals were high and close to those reported in the HERA trial. With a median follow-up of 32 months, 107 breast cancer relapses were recorded (overall frequency, 10.67 %), and lymph node involvement, estrogen receptor negativity, lymphoid infiltration, and vascular invasion were identified as independent prognostic factors for tumor recurrence, indicating that relapses were associated with advanced tumor stage. Analysis of site and frequency of distant metastases showed that bone metastases were significantly more frequent during or immediately after trastuzumab (<18 months from the start of treatment) compared to recurrences in bone after the end of treatment and wash-out of the drug (>18 months from the start of treatment) (35.89 vs. 14.28 %, p = 0.0240); no significant differences were observed in recurrences in the other recorded body sites, raising the possibility that the protection exerted by trastuzumab is lower in bone metastases.

title: Early Diagnostic Procedure and Treatment for Invasive Fungal Infection Centered on Invasive Aspergillosis in Patients with Myelodysplastic Syndrome or Acute Myeloid Leukemia
abstract: Abstract Abstract 1544 Since myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are more prevalent in the elderly, intensive chemotherapy is difficult. However, recent progress in supportive therapy, especially with anti-fungal agents, and diagnostic procedures for invasive fungal infection (IFI) such as β-D glucan (β-D), galactomannan antigen (GM) and computed tomography (CT), have resulted in dramatically enhanced safety of post-chemotherapy control of elderly patients. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of our diagnosis and treatment strategy for IFI, we examined 112 consecutive episodes in 110 patients who received remission induction therapy from December 15, 2009 to June 18, 2011, including new or recurrent patients with MDS related AML (MDS-AML) and those with AML without a history of invasive aspergillosis (IA). Diagnosis was MDS-AML in 88 episodes (relapse 18) and AML in 24 (M1 5,M2 9,M4 9,M6 1).The median age was 70 (range: 21–88). Remission induction therapy consisted of behenoyl-ara-C for 10 days and idarubicin for 4 days (For further details, please refer to 51st ASH abstract #1052; Taiichi Kyo et al). Patients were always admitted to a clean room until neutrophil recovery, and were routinely administered macrophage-colony stimulating factor (CSF) and granulocyte-CSF. Amphotericin-b syrup and itraconazole capsules were given as antifungal prophylaxis. IFI diagnostic procedures consisted of CT, GM, β-D and surveillance culture (SC). At the time of admission a control CT was taken. CT was repeated within 24 hours when pyrexia of ≥38.0°C occurred. If fever showed no improvement, CT was repeated every 3 days (X-ray was also taken). If any change suggesting infection was noted, treatment against IA was considered. GM, β-D and SC were all conducted twice a week from the time of admission until discharge. ≥0.5 GM was regarded as positive and the treatment against IA was started even if there was only one positive result. At present there is no worldwide consensus concerning β-D, thus we considered a value exceeding the cut-off value of the reagent as positive. Treatment was started when there were both a positive result and increasing fever; and treatment against IA or candidiasis depended on imaging findings. Even if β-D was negative, candida detected by SC or diarrhea combined with increasing fever was also an indication for treatment against candidiasis. IA was treated with voriconazole (VRCZ) and candidiasis with micafungin (MCFG). VRCZ and MCFC were administered at 200–300 mg/twice/day and 100–300 mg/day, respectively. When no sufficient effect was observed with VRCZ alone, MCFG was added. Complete remission (CR) and partial remission (PR) were achieved in 81/112 (72%) and 9/112 (8%) episodes, while in 19/112 (17%) no response was obtained and 3/112 (2.7%) episodes resulted in death during chemotherapy. CR rate was comparable among de novo MDS-AML (49/70, 70%), MDS-AML relapse (9/18, 50%) and AML (23/24, 96%). The cause of death associated with chemotherapy was bacteremia 1, bacteremia or IA 1, and cerebral hemorrhage 1. GM was positive in 48 (43%) episodes. The reason for this large number was probably the advanced age of the patients and the long term neutropenia [absolute neutrophil count <500 (median) 27 days]. In spite of higher IA morbidity, mortality rates seemed very low. Furthermore, although GM >2.5 indicates an unfavorable prognosis and >5.0 no hope of survival, none of our patients with GM >2.5 (10 patients) died of IA (2 died of other causes) and all patients with GM >5.0 (4 patients) survived. Candidemia was found in 2 patients (krusei 1, guilliermondii 1) and were treated succesfully. β-D was positive in 46 /112 (41%) episodes and 28/112 (25%) were also positive for GM. As for GM and β-D, GM positivity preceded that of β-D in 9/28 (32%); regarding GM and CT, GM positivity preceded the observation of CT findings in 13/30 (43%). At the beginning of this study, no control CT was obtained. But in the course of the study we found some patients who presented CT findings indicating IA, such as nodular lesions, but with no infection. Thus, we realized the need for a control CT to detect IA more accurately. Each diagnostic procedure has excellent characteristics but it is not sufficient by itself. The results of this single-center clinical study indicate that an improvement of antifungal therapy combined with a battery of diagnostic procedures may allow safe, intensive chemotherapy for many patients with MDS or AML. Disclosures: No relevant conflicts of interest to declare.

title: Issues to debate on the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) study: Hormone replacement therapy and acute coronary outcomes: methodological issues between randomized and observational studies
abstract: A large number of observational studies, supported by animal and basic research studies, have shown a protective effect of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) on acute coronary outcomes. The recent large randomized Women's Health Initiative (WHI) study reported the opposite result, i.e. a small risk increase of 29% for acute coronary outcomes under estrogen-progestin treatment. Possible methodological reasons for these discrepancies are discussed. Despite randomization, the reported small increase in risk in the WHI study could be spurious because of differential unblinding of HRT users, which could have resulted in higher detection rates of otherwise clinically unrecognized acute myocardial infarction in these women. We show that altering diagnostic patterns because of unblinding could lower the crude rate ratio of 1.28 to 1.02. In the observational studies, the protective effect may have been exaggerated due to a healthy user bias and to the inappropriate choice of the reference group. Using an alternative reference group, the combined rate ratio of 0.67 was increased to 0.82. The diametrical effects of HRT on acute coronary outcomes found between the observational studies and the WHI Study may be a result not only of bias in the observational studies, but also of bias in the WHI Study.

title: The Diagnostic Dyad: Machiavelli, Kafka, and the Equilibrium Ledger
abstract: This paper is the tenth empirical study in the Attractor Portraits series and closes the programme’s first historical arc by turning from the analysis of concentrated actors and systems to the diagnosticians who perceive their structural logic. Niccolò Machiavelli and Franz Kafka are treated as a Diagnostic Dyad: two historically separated but analytically complementary figures whose work describes opposite ends of the same civilisational process. Machiavelli diagnoses concentrated sovereign power at the moment of its formation; Kafka diagnoses the procedural and bureaucratic residue that remains after personal sovereignty has been dispersed into institutional systems. The paper develops the Diagnostic Primary as a distinct attractor configuration. The Diagnostic Primary is characterised by maximum or near-maximum Systemic Coherence combined with extremely low Capital Density, high symbolic portability, and a disproportionate increase in Psychic Energy after death. The Attractor Density Index is applied independently to the two cases. Machiavelli is provisionally assessed at ADI 7.20, comprising SC 9.0, PE 8.0, CD 2.0, and CF 8.5. Kafka is assessed at ADI 7.70, comprising SC 9.5, PE 9.5, CD 1.0, and CF 9.0. The moderate aggregate scores conceal an unusual dimensional structure: very high cognitive and symbolic coherence exists without the institutional and material insulation that amplifies other attractor types. This dimensional profile is compared with Alan Turing’s earlier configuration and used to test whether high Systemic Coherence combined with near-zero Capital Density forms a recurring diagnostic type across radically different historical fields. The paper argues that Diagnostic Primaries concentrate through systemic perception rather than institutional construction. Their principal output is not an organisation, dynasty, infrastructure, or state but a conceptual architecture through which the field becomes capable of perceiving itself. Their posthumous influence may therefore substantially exceed the concentration visible during their lifetimes. Machiavelli is analysed as the programme’s proto-Ledger diagnostician. His concepts of virtù and fortuna are read as an early structural grammar for the interaction between internal attractor capacity and unstable field conditions. His political analysis is interpreted not as a moral endorsement of particular forms of power but as an empirical attempt to understand how concentration is produced, maintained, destabilised, and corrected under changing environmental conditions. The paper therefore places Machiavelli within the genealogy of the Equilibrium Ledger’s account of concentration, structural readiness, instability, and corrective return. Kafka occupies the opposite side of the Diagnostic Dyad. Where Machiavelli asks how power concentrates, Kafka asks what concentrated power becomes after it has dissolved into administrative procedure. The Trial and The Castle are analysed as literary maps of institutional thermodynamics: procedural opacity, inaccessible legitimacy, distributed responsibility, administrative abstraction, and systemic guilt as experienced from inside the human nervous system. Kafka thereby provides a phenomenology of the institutional field that emerges when sovereign command is replaced by procedure and when power no longer requires a visible individual centre. The relationship between Machiavelli and Kafka is therefore developed as a before-and-after image of political modernity. Machiavelli observes power becoming concentrated in the prince and the state. Kafka observes the residue of that concentration after successive institutional settlements have converted personal sovereignty into administrative systems whose authority is dispersed, difficult to locate, and frequently impossible for the individual to contest directly. The Equilibrium Ledger is positioned analytically between these two diagnostic poles: between the concentration event and the institutional residue it leaves behind. The paper introduces three new structural instruments. The first is the Sarcastic Shield, formalised as the Decoupling Mechanism: the use of irony, satire, and comic distance as a cognitive pressure valve through which structurally difficult observations can be processed without carrying their full emotional load simultaneously. Machiavelli’s La Mandragola and Kafka’s dark bureaucratic humour are treated as different manifestations of the same underlying mechanism. The instrument reframes humour not merely as style but as a possible cognitive survival technology under conditions of sustained diagnostic exposure. The second instrument is the Biological Choke Point, formalised as the Extraction Cost of the Surplus Mind. It identifies the point at which sustained cognitive surplus processing and institutional extraction exceed the biological substrate’s capacity for continued compensation. The paper expressly distinguishes structural analysis from mystical or simplistic medical causation: Machiavelli’s torture and Kafka’s tuberculosis remain historically and biologically contingent events. The proposed analytical question concerns the relationship between sustained institutional extraction, unresolved interpretive labour, biological expenditure, and the vulnerability of the diagnostic node. The third instrument is the Night Study as Cognitive Clean Room, formalised as Temporal Decoupling. Machiavelli’s nocturnal study at Sant’Andrea and Kafka’s night writing are analysed as independently developed temporal architectures in which secondary cognitive processing becomes possible after the institutional demands of the day have been removed. The paper defines the Decoupling Threshold as the transition between institutional processing and secondary cognitive production, and the Cognitive Clean Room as the temporal or environmental space in which unresolved structural material can be processed with reduced institutional noise. These mechanisms converge in the paper’s account of the Surplus Mind. The Surplus Mind is not defined by intellectual superiority or simple cognitive speed. It is defined by continuous unresolved interpretive labour: sustained processing of structural contradictions that surrounding institutions normalise, suppress, or fail to perceive. Machiavelli and Kafka are treated as historically distinct manifestations of this configuration, converting unresolved institutional contradiction into analytical or literary forms whose civilisational value becomes substantially more visible after their deaths. The paper also extends the Institutional Mythologisation Cycle through two opposed posthumous transformations. Machiavelli undergoes mythological inversion: the diagnostician of power becomes culturally compressed into the adjective “Machiavellian,” frequently detached from the analytical complexity of his work. Kafka undergoes mythological sanctification: the diagnostician of bureaucratic opacity becomes the prophetic figure encoded in “Kafkaesque.” In both cases, the individual name becomes a portable structural category while the field simplifies the intellectual architecture that produced it. Portrait No. 10 then performs the programme’s first sustained recursive application of its instruments to the structural conditions of the Equilibrium Ledger’s own production. The paper identifies three methodological dangers in this operation: narcissistic collapse, in which structural analysis becomes personal mythology; deterministic collapse, in which theory is reduced to biography; and epistemic collapse, in which recursive self-analysis contaminates the diagnostic instrument through motivated reasoning or infinite regress. Rather than claiming to resolve these dangers completely, the paper treats them as explicit methodological constraints. The validity of the framework’s propositions is separated from the biography of the person who developed them: biographical and institutional conditions may explain why particular contradictions became perceptually salient, but they do not establish whether the resulting theoretical claims are true. That question remains evidential and comparative. Recursive self-application is therefore presented as an experiment in methodological transparency rather than as proof of the framework’s validity. The Diagnostic Dyad consequently performs two functions within the wider research programme. Historically, it connects the analysis of concentrated political power with the later development of procedural and administrative power. Methodologically, it forces the Equilibrium Ledger to subject its own production conditions to the same structural scrutiny it applies to external cases. Machiavelli supplies the discipline of structural analysis without moral romanticisation; Kafka supplies the phenomenological record of what institutional contradiction costs the individual who cannot cease perceiving it. The paper concludes that diagnostic cognition constitutes a distinctive form of concentration whose field effects cannot be measured adequately through material or institutional capital alone. Machiavelli and Kafka demonstrate how low-capital nodes may generate exceptionally durable conceptual infrastructures, and how institutional exclusion, temporal decoupling, symbolic portability, and posthumous mythologisation interact within the Diagnostic Primary configuration. Portrait No. 10 therefore closes the first arc of Attractor Portraits by converting the framework itself from observer into object of observation and by establishing the Diagnostic Dyad as the bridge from historical sovereign concentration to the procedural institutions examined
